data.title: Parties to negotiate after no one wins majority in New Zealand election
data.description:
New Zealand's ruling coalition fell short of winning a parliamentary majority, final results of the November 7 election showed on Friday, leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon needing the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to form government.

Luxon said his centre-right National Party would work with its coalition partners, ACT and New Zealand First, and Opportunity to form government and avoid the need for a fresh election.

Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong said she would negotiate with National as the party with the largest number of seats. That was consistent with statements she made before the election result was known. However, she has also said previously that Opportunity was prepared to speak with other parties.

WHERE DO THINGS STAND?

The final vote count showed the incumbent coalition of National, the right-wing ACT Party and the nationalist New Zealand First won 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, one short of a majority, according to the Electoral Commission results.

Opportunity, contesting its first election, won seven seats.

On the left, Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori hold 58 seats. This would not be enough seats to form a government even with the support of Opportunity.

The possibility remains that parties from either bloc could join forces to create a majority, such as in 2017 when Labour and NZ First reached a deal that made Jacinda Ardern prime minister.

WHAT IS THE PROCESS?

While there have been some informal meetings between parties since the election, now that the parties know how many seats they need to form a ​government, more formal negotiations can begin.

Along with policies, key ministerial appointments such as deputy prime minister, foreign minister and finance minister can all be part of negotiations.

Parties can sign either coalition agreements or looser alliances known as confidence-and-supply agreements. Under ​those deals, a smaller party agrees to support a government on key votes, without taking cabinet seats or being part of the government.

WHEN MIGHT NEW ZEALAND GET ​A GOVERNMENT?

Coalition negotiations lasted 40 days after the 2023 election, with National, ACT and New Zealand First signing their agreements on November 24. If negotiations follow a similar time frame, a government could be formed before Christmas.

However, since New Zealand introduced a proportional electoral system in 1996, only coalitions of up to three parties have ever been needed to form a majority. With four parties needing to reach agreement, it could take longer.

Parliament has to meet six weeks after the writs are returned. If no recounts are ordered, writs will be returned on December 3 and parliament must meet on or before January 14.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER SIX WEEKS?

If a government hasn't been formed, parliament will still meet and lawmakers will be sworn in and a speaker elected.

The following day, parliament would be officially opened, the governor-general would deliver a speech and then a lawmaker could move to adjourn the house. This would mean that negotiations to form government could continue.

Governor-General Cindy Kiro said in a speech earlier this year that if it became clear that no government could be formed, another election may be required.

"The caretaker Prime Minister would be expected to consult other parties and seek majority support for calling a new election," she said.

WHO IS IN CHARGE UNTIL ​THEN?

The incumbent ⁠government, the National-led coalition, will continue to operate as a caretaker government while the new government is formed.

According to New Zealand's parliamentary website, a caretaker government can continue the normal business of the country but cannot make any significant ​decisions on its own except in an emergency or crisis.

data.title: Axis Bank leads India's October credit card rush in its first Apple Pay month - IntelliNews Lambda
data.description:
IntelliNews summary:

  • Card spending rose 20.1% m/m and 14.4% y/y to INR2.45 trillion ($26.4bn) as the festive season began.
  • HDFC Bank added only 52,478 cards, against 280,353 in September, though it remains the largest issuer with 27.43mn.
  • SBI Card and ICICI Bank each added more than 200,000 cards; slice Small Finance Bank added 100,280.
  • The RBI's 2023 increase in card risk weights still stands, but delinquencies have eased and issuance is picking up.

____________________

Axis Bank led India's lenders in net credit card additions in October, its first full month as Apple Pay's only bank partner, as market leader HDFC Bank nearly stalled.

Indian banks had 126.72mn credit cards in issue at the end of October, a net gain of 1,400,814 in the month, according to the Reserve Bank of India's bank-wise card statistics published on November 20. That is more than twice the 626,325 added in October 2025 and the biggest monthly increase in at least 13 months. Spending on cards jumped 20.1% from September and 14.4% from a year earlier to INR2.45 trillion.

Axis Bank's base grew by 281,705 to 16.84mn, a fifth of the industry's net gain and nearly three and a half times the 79,842 it managed a year earlier. Its customers spent INR302.11bn on their cards, 23.8% more than a year earlier and 30.5% more than in September, lifting its share of national card spending to 12.3% from 11.4%.

With 127mn cards in a country of 1.4bn people, credit remains largely the preserve of better-off urban India, and card data are the clearest monthly gauge of how freely the middle class is borrowing to spend. October's surge suggests issuers are opening the taps again after two years of caution imposed by the central bank, just as a foreign wallet tests whether it can win share in a market built around the domestic UPI instant-payment network.

Net additions to credit cards outstanding in India, thousands, all banks, October 2025 to October 2026. Source: Reserve Bank of India, bank-wise ATM/POS/card statistics (provisional). IntelliNews

A tap-to-pay test

Apple switched on its wallet in India on September 30, and its launch release named only Axis Bank's Visa and Mastercard credit cards as eligible. Cards on RuPay, the domestic network that can be linked to UPI, were left out, as were debit cards.

'India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy,' said Jennifer Bailey, Apple's vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet.

HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and SBI Card were still negotiating when the service went live, with Apple asking for about 20 basis points on each transaction, TechCrunch reported on September 29.

The wallet cannot claim the whole of Axis Bank's spurt. The lender had already added 259,525 cards in September, up from 32,789 in August, before Apple Pay went live, and the RBI tables say nothing about why customers signed up.

HDFC Bank pauses

HDFC Bank, the largest issuer with 27.43mn cards, added just 52,478 in October, down from 280,353 in September and 144,419 a year earlier. That was its smallest monthly gain since March, when it added 52,420. Spending on its cards rose 13.2% year-on-year to INR701.15bn, but only 7.6% month-on-month, well behind the industry, and its share of national spending slipped to 28.6% from 28.9%.

SBI Card added 255,338 cards to reach 23.42mn, with spending up 14.5% y/y at INR457.97bn. ICICI Bank, which had added fewer than 30,000 in September, put on 212,758 to reach 20.08mn, although its card spending grew only 6.9% y/y to INR422.96bn. Further down the table, state-owned Bank of Baroda added 114,663 cards and the fintech-backed slice Small Finance Bank 100,280, nearly four times the 26,257 cards it had in issue a year earlier.

Net additions to credit cards outstanding by issuer, thousands, September and October 2026. SBI Card's cards are reported under State Bank of India. Source: Reserve Bank of India, bank-wise ATM/POS/card statistics (provisional). IntelliNews

Festivals arrive late

Navratri began on October 11 this year and Diwali fell on November 8, whereas in 2025 the festive season opened on September 22, the same day as a cut in goods and services tax, and Diwali came on October 20. Flipkart's Big Billion Days sale was unveiled on October 9. A year ago card users had loaded up online in the September festivities, which pushed spending that month to a record.

October 2026 therefore captured the opening weeks of the season, while its comparison month already contained Diwali itself, which makes 14.4% y/y growth respectable rather than spectacular. November's figures, which will cover Diwali, are the better test of household demand.

Credit card spending in India at PoS terminals, online and other, INR trillion a month, all banks, October 2025 to October 2026. Source: Reserve Bank of India, bank-wise ATM/POS/card statistics (provisional). IntelliNews

The brakes come off, slowly

Issuers spent much of the past two years on the defensive. In a November 2023 circular, the RBI increased the risk weight on banks' card receivables by 25 percentage points to 150%, and on non-bank lenders' to 125%. A February 2025 circular eased the separate rule on bank lending to non-bank financial companies, but left the card risk weights in place. Card defaults had risen to 7.6% of portfolios by mid-2024 and growth in the card base slowed to about 8% a year by March 2026.

Net 90-day-plus delinquency on cards fell to 1.56% in December 2025 from 1.93% a year earlier, Equifax India said in February, and in its June report it found new issuance down 9% y/y in the first quarter even as card balances grew and arrears eased. The card base is now 11.0% bigger than a year ago.

Tanay Dalal, an economist at Axis Bank, warned in early November that consumption is being propped up by subsidies and debt, with unsecured bank lending growing about 30% y/y. Cheap instalment loans for phones and appliances are also drawing first-time borrowers into formal credit, and card offers tend to follow. With cleaner books and Diwali spending still to be counted, issuers have room to keep pushing cards, and Apple still needs one of the big three to sign.

data.title: Inside VinFast’s Net-Zero Climate Commitment
data.description:
While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.

One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast’s September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.

Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers

For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove’s proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem’s charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.

VinFast’s buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately 2,000 of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast’s experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.

“Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market,” said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.

For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company’s U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.

In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.

Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura’s Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.

Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change

VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam’s best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup’s annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.

Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast’s 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.

VinFast’s emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.

How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice

VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company’s stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.

In January 2025, VinFast’s chairwoman approved the company’s net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.

  • Electrification. VinFast plans to electrify equipment at company-owned production and business sites by 2030. The roadmap also includes expanding access to charging and developing battery energy storage.

  • Energy Saving. VinFast plans to introduce smart energy monitoring at manufacturing facilities by 2028. Monitoring production lines and major electricity-consuming equipment gives factory teams more detailed information on where energy is used and where operations can be made more efficient.

  • Energy Greening. VinFast aims to use 100% renewable electricity at all its plants by 2040. Its roadmap includes rooftop solar, battery storage to support renewable power use, and work with suppliers on lower-emission materials.

VinFast’s manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.

The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.

Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.

The company is actively expanding its distribution and dealership network globally, while growing manufacturing capacity across key markets in North America, Europe and Asia.
